Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 67
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: School Principal
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Shouting: Shouting, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study, Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Arthur is a sixty-seven-year-old married man who has served as the principal of a mid-sized public high school for the past fourteen years. He came to therapy at the urging of his wife, who had grown increasingly worried about his withdrawal, irritability, and the way he would startle at the slightest unexpected sound. For Arthur, the trouble began eighteen months ago, on a rainy November evening, when he was driving home from a school board meeting. A driver ran a red light and T-boned his sedan at an intersection. Arthur remembers the impact—the shriek of metal, the glass exploding inward—but the moments immediately after are a blur of sirens and fluorescent lights. He was hospitalized for three days with a broken clavicle and several cracked ribs, but the physical injuries healed. What has not healed is the way the event lives inside him.

Arthur cannot put the experience into words. When his wife asks him to describe what he felt during the crash, he shakes his head and says he just can’t. The memory is not a story he can tell; it is a film that plays without his permission. At unpredictable moments—while standing in the hallway between classes, while sitting at his desk reviewing a schedule—the image of the other car’s headlights rushing toward his window flashes before him, and for a terrifying second he is back in that driver’s seat, his hands gripping the wheel, his chest seizing with the impact. He feels the collision happening right now, his heart hammering, his breath catching, his body bracing for a blow that has already come. He has come to believe that he has permanently changed for the worse. Before the crash, he was a decisive, steady presence in the school. Now he sees himself as fragile, diminished. He is certain that somebody else—a stronger person—would never have gotten into this situation in the first place, as though the crash were a judgment on his own inadequacy.

The world, Arthur now believes, is a dangerous place, and he monitors it constantly. He has developed a peculiar sensitivity to delays. If a teacher is late for a meeting, if a bus does not arrive at the expected time, his mind immediately races to catastrophe: an accident, a death, something terrible unfolding that he cannot stop. He cannot relax, even in his own living room, even when his wife tells him everything is fine. His sleep is fractured; he lies awake for hours, listening to the house settle, or he wakes at three in the morning with his heart pounding and no memory of a dream. The triggers are everywhere. A student shouting in the hallway makes him flinch as though a car horn is blaring. The sound of a door slamming, a chair scraping too loudly, a dropped textbook—all of it sends a jolt through him. He has become especially vigilant around cars. When he sees a vehicle that has been in a minor fender-bender, or even a car parked crookedly, his stomach drops and he has to look away.

To manage the distress, Arthur has developed habits that he knows are not helping but that feel necessary in the moment. He forces himself to think only positive thoughts, telling himself over and over that everything is fine, that he is safe, that nothing bad is happening. But the effort exhausts him, and the relief never lasts. At home, he eats excessively in the evenings—bags of chips, leftovers, whatever is within reach—as a way to quiet the restlessness that builds inside him. The most consequential strategy, though, is his avoidance of work. He used to arrive at school by seven and stay until six, walking the halls, greeting students, solving problems as they arose. Now he arrives as late as he can, leaves as early as he can, and spends as much time as possible in his office with the door closed. He has delegated tasks he once handled himself. His assistant principal has noticed, and has begun to ask pointed questions. Arthur knows he is withdrawing from a job he once loved, and the shame of it only deepens his conviction that he is no longer the man he used to be.

What finally brought Arthur to seek help was a morning last month when a fire drill alarm went off unexpectedly. He was in the main office, and the sound—loud, sudden, piercing—sent him into a full-blown panic. He ducked behind his desk, heart racing, certain he was about to die. A secretary found him there, pale and shaking. He made an excuse about low blood sugar, but he knew, and she knew, that something was seriously wrong. His wife insisted he call a therapist, and he agreed, partly because he was afraid of what might happen next. He is hoping, though he would not say it aloud, that someone can help him find a way back to the person he was before the crash—the principal who walked the halls without flinching, the husband who could sit still in his own home. He is terrified that the permanent damage he feels is real, and that no amount of talking will undo it.
